title: Unravelling time-resolved Interparticle Coulombic Decay: From spectral formation to decay lifetimes
authors: Alexander V. Riegel, Max K. Humm, Jan-Thore Kahle, Elke Fasshauer
abstract: Electronic decay processes provide a fascinating window into correlated electronic rearrangements occurring on ultrafast timescales. Following these dynamics in real time has become increasingly accessible experimentally, but extracting the underlying electronic dynamics from measured spectra requires understanding how nuclear motion shapes the observable signal. Here, we extend an analytical description of time-resolved electronic decay spectra to include dissociative nuclear dynamics and apply it to Interparticle Coulombic Decay (ICD) in the neon dimer. The resulting spectra reproduce the experimentally observed spectral shape and reveal an unexpectedly important role of interference between pathways involving different vibronic resonance states. We further establish a clear connection between the temporal build-up of the spectral structure and the nuclear wavepacket dynamics in the decaying electronic state. Most strikingly, our analytical expressions reveal that the time-dependent integrated ICD signal contains contributions proportional to both $\exp(-t/τ)$ and $\exp[-t/(2τ)]$. Nevertheless, a conventional mono-exponential fit can describe the temporal signal remarkably well while yielding a decay lifetime that differs substantially from the underlying value. Applying the theoretically derived fitting model to experimental data for the neon dimer yields an ICD lifetime $τ$ of 73 fs, rather than the previously extracted 150(50) fs, placing the experimental value within the range of previous theoretical predictions. Since the underlying temporal structure is common to electronic decay processes, our findings have implications for extracting lifetimes from time-resolved decay spectra well beyond ICD.
summary: The research analyzes time-resolved Interparticle Coulombic Decay (ICD) by coupling electronic decay theory with dissociative nuclear motion. The authors demonstrate that extracting the true decay lifetime requires careful consideration of the underlying temporal structure, as simple exponential fitting can lead to erroneous results. This provides a crucial methodological guide for interpreting ultrafast spectroscopy in molecular physics.
main_problem: The study aims to accurately extract the true decay lifetime ($\tau$) governing time-resolved Interparticle Coulombic Decay (ICD) by correctly modeling the influence of dissociative nuclear dynamics on the measured electronic spectrum.
main_result: A conventional mono-exponential fit can yield a significantly different lifetime than the underlying physical value; applying a more complex fitting model yields an ICD lifetime ($\tau \approx 73$ fs) consistent with previous theoretical predictions.
method: The authors developed and applied an analytical description of time-resolved electronic decay spectra, extending it to include dissociative nuclear dynamics, and compared results from mono-exponential versus double-exponential fitting models.
model_or_system: The system is the neon dimer undergoing ICD following photoionization. The theoretical framework involves solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with a Hamiltonian partitioned into non-decaying, coupling, and light-matter interaction terms, incorporating repulsive Coulomb potentials for the final state continuum.
key_observables: Time-resolved ICD electron spectrum $P(E_{\text{kin}}, E_p, t)$ and the integrated decay signal vs. time ($t$).
important_parameters: Decay lifetime ($\tau$), internuclear distance ($R$), photoelectron energy ($E_p$), and kinetic energy of the emitted ICD electron ($E_{\text{kin}}$).
main_assumptions: Key approximations include assuming a product ansatz for the total state, approximating the coupling matrix element factorization, and ignoring interactions between emitted electrons in the continuum.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates energy levels and decay pathways (direct vs. resonance); Figure 2 shows the repulsive Coulomb potential and associated eigenfunctions; later figures compare experimental data fits using different exponential models.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the theoretical framework for time-resolved ICD spectra, detailing the necessary analytical extensions to include nuclear motion, presenting the results of fitting simulated/experimental data with various decay functions, and concluding with implications for general lifetime extraction techniques.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the complex interplay between electronic excitation dynamics and molecular structure (nuclear wavepacket evolution) in ultrafast processes, which is a core theme in advanced AMO physics and quantum optics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (Colour online) Schematic illustration [51] of energy levels and processes in a diatomic system. Lower curve: elec- tronic ground state hosting one bound vibrational state |χ0⟩; upper curve: electronic resonance state hosting Nλ bound vibrational states |χλ⟩; middle curve: dissociative electronic final state hosting a continuum of nuclear states |χµ⟩. Possi- ble pathways into a given final state: direct pathway (dashed arrow); resonance pathways (solid arrows), both leading to emission of electron with kinetic energy Ekin (dashed double- headed arrows).

FIG. 2. (Colour online) Repulsive Coulomb nuclear potential Eq. (11) of the final state (orange) with a selection of energy- normalized nuclear Coulomb eigenfunctions Eq. (12) (blue). Energies are chosen for constant steps ∆R in the internuclear distance R which correspond to non-uniformly distributed en- ergies (dashed black lines) to better sample the region of in- terest.

FIG. 3. (Colour online) The PECs used to model the neon dimer. Top: PECs for the resonance state (blue curve), and for the final state (orange curve). The resonance state hosts 11 bound vibrational states |χλ⟩; the lowest and highest of their energy levels are indicated between their respective classical turning points (green dashed lines). Bottom: PEC for the electronic ground state (violet curve). The energetic level of the vibrational ground state |χ0⟩is indicated between the classical turning points (violet dashed line) and serves as the reference point for the energy scale.

(Colour online) ICD electron spectrum (blue curve) as function of the kinetic energy of the secondary electron, Ekin, at constant time t = 1 ps and kinetic energy of the photoelectron, Ep = 9.754 eV. The ionizing laser pulse has FWHM of 6 fs. The overall structure is physical (orange curve on top, see Sec. IV B), the fine structure is an artefact due to the discretization of the continuum of nuclear final states in steps of 0.01 ˚A, see main text.

FIG. 5. (Colour online) ICD signal intensity (dark blue solid line) as a function of the kinetic energy of the photoelectron, Ep, at constant time t = 1 ps and kinetic energy of the ICD electron, Ekin = 0 eV. The ionizing laser pulse has FWHM of 6 fs. The spectral shape can be closely fitted to a Gaussian function (orange dashed line). Spectrum for the pulse with FWHM of 60 fs shown for comparison (violet solid line), a few data points affected by numerical noise have been discarded and the spectrum has been scaled up.
